chapter.title: Choosing who to watch and where to look

cards.body: Your clipping service could read 50 newspapers every morning. The weak link is you, reading the note it leaves. Watch 40 pages, and by Friday you've stopped opening the note. The fix: **3 to 5 rivals, and only the 1 or 2 pages each where their news actually breaks**.
cards.simpler: Imagine a clipping service that could read 50 newspapers every morning. The slow part is you, reading the note it leaves behind. If you watch 40 pages, by Friday you've usually stopped opening the note. The fix is to watch **3 to 5 rivals, and only the 1 or 2 pages each where their news actually breaks**.

cards.prompt: You hire a real person to clip stories about your rivals. Which instruction gets you a note you'll still be reading next month?

options.text: Read every page of all 30 local papers, every morning.
Read the business pages of these 5 papers, every morning.
Read the front page of one paper, once a month.

whyNot.a: That's the 40-things trap, not a watch list: the note would be too long to read before your coffee goes cold.
whyNot.c: That's too little, not too focused: once a month, you'd hear about a price change weeks after your customers did.

cards.reteach: A good clipper is useful because of what they leave out. Point them at a few sections where news really happens, and the note stays short enough to read every morning.

cards.title: Rivals first, then pages
cards.body:
Start with people. Pick the 3 to 5 rivals your customers actually mention: the name on a lost sale, the tab open next to yours. The famous giant in your space can wait.

Then pick pages, not whole websites. A *page* is one web address, like example.com/pricing. Four kinds earn their place: **pricing, changelog, blog and careers**. A *changelog* is the list of product updates. Each of these moves when the company moves.

The home page is the trap. It's the shop window: polished, and when it changes, it's usually a new banner or photo, not news.
cards.simpler: Start with people, then pages. Pick the 3 to 5 rivals your customers mention: the name on a lost sale, the tab open next to yours. The famous giant can wait. Next, pick pages, each one web address like example.com/pricing. Four kinds change when the company changes: **pricing, changelog, blog and careers**. A changelog is the list of product updates. Skip the home page. Like a shop window, it's polished, and its changes are usually a new banner or photo, not news.

cards.title: Priya's 6 addresses
cards.body: Priya sells a booking app to yoga studios. Her first list had 41 addresses, and she stopped reading the results by Thursday. Her second list had 6: 3 real rivals, 2 pages each. In week two, one rival's careers page listed 2 new jobs for payments engineers. Their blog said nothing about payments for another month. Priya found out first because she was reading the most boring page on their site.
cards.simpler: Priya sells a booking app to yoga studios. Her first list had 41 web addresses, and by Thursday she had stopped reading what came back. Her second list had 6: 3 real rivals, 2 pages each. In week two, one rival's careers page showed 2 new jobs for payments engineers. Their blog said nothing about payments for another month. Priya knew first because **she was reading the most boring page on their site**.

cards.prompt: You're watching Brightline, a rival note-taking app. You have room for one more page. Which one?

whyNot.a: That's the shop window, not the stockroom: home page changes are often new banners or tested headlines, and rarely tell you what the company is doing.
whyNot.c: That's history, not news: an About page tells you where they've been, and it almost never moves.

cards.reteach: Ask which page moves when the company moves. A changelog gets a new line every time they ship something. Home and About pages are built to look good, not to report news.

cards.title: Why fewer wins
cards.body:
Why not 50? Every page you add is a page you have to read about tomorrow. At 50 pages, Monday's note is three screens of footer dates and cookie banners, and the one price change is buried on screen two. **Fewer pages, read every day, beat many pages skimmed.**

Michael Porter's book *Competitive Strategy* gives a good test. It says to know 4 things about a rival: their goals, current strategy, assumptions and capabilities. Here's one way to match your pages to them (our reading, not Porter's). Pricing shows strategy. The changelog shows capabilities. Careers hint at goals. The blog can hint at their assumptions.

Next to each address, write one line saying which of the 4 it shows. No line, no page.
cards.simpler: Each added page is one more to read tomorrow. At 50 pages, Monday's note is three screens of footer dates and cookie banners, with the one price change buried on screen two. **Fewer pages, read every day, beat many pages skimmed.** Michael Porter's book *Competitive Strategy* says to know a rival's goals, strategy, assumptions and capabilities. One way to match pages to them (our reading, not Porter's): pricing shows strategy, the changelog shows capabilities, careers hint at goals, the blog can hint at assumptions. Next to each address, write which one it shows. No line, no page.

cards.body: Tom adds every rival's social accounts, help docs and full site map: 38 addresses. His first summary runs 4 screens, mostly cookie banners and a new date in a footer. By Friday he has muted it. The warning sign: if you can't say in one line why a page is on the list, it's noise in a nice suit.
cards.simpler: Tom adds every rival's social accounts, help pages and full site map: 38 addresses. His first summary runs 4 screens long, mostly cookie banners and a new date at the bottom of a page. By Friday he has muted it. Here's the warning sign: if you can't say in one line why a page is on the list, **it's noise in a nice suit**.

cards.prompt: What earns a page a spot on your watch list?

options.text: It's the most visited page on the rival's site.
It changes when the rival makes a move, and you can say what it shows.
It's long, so the agent has plenty to read.

whyNot.a: That's popularity, not news: the most visited page is usually the home page, which mostly shows polish, not moves.
whyNot.c: That's volume, not value: more text makes a longer note, not a better one.

cards.reteach: Think of each page as a newspaper section you pay someone to read. Keep it only if it changes when the rival acts, and you can name what it tells you: goals, strategy, assumptions or capabilities.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Watch 3 to 5 real rivals, and only the 1 or 2 pages each that move when the company moves: pricing, changelog, blog, careers. If you can't say in one line why a page is on the list, cut it.
cards.simpler: Watch 3 to 5 real rivals. For each, watch only the 1 or 2 pages that change when the company changes: pricing, changelog, blog or careers. **If you can't say in one line why a page is on the list, cut it.**

cards.body:
Write down your 3 closest rivals. For each, find their pricing page plus one of changelog, blog or careers. Paste the 6 addresses into a note, each with one line saying why it's there.

Tomorrow: your agent saves its first clipping, and learns some pages fight back.
cards.simpler: Write down your 3 closest rivals. For each one, find their pricing page plus one more: their changelog, blog or careers page. A changelog is their list of product updates. Paste the 6 addresses into a note, **each with one line saying why it's there**. Tomorrow, your agent saves its first clipping, and learns that some pages fight back.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write a list of 3 to 5 competitors with 1 or 2 exact web addresses each, and say why each page is worth reading.

dubious_claims: 'Most competitor tracking dies in its first week from watching 40 pages' is an invented-sounding statistic with no source

'Home pages change rarely and say little when they do' (card 5 feedback) is shaky, because many software companies change their home page headline and banners often for A/B tests (showing different versions to different visitors) and launches

The way Porter's four things are matched to pages ('the blog shows what they believe' = assumptions) is the author's own reading, not Porter's. The four parts themselves (goals, current strategy, assumptions, capabilities) are correct for Competitive Strategy (1980)
repairedFrom.why: 'Why fewer wins' is the longest teach card and has no concrete image. Its first half is abstract talk about notes going unread, and the Porter list arrives as a second idea with no picture to hold it.
repairedFrom.fix: Replace 'At 50 pages, even a quiet week makes a long note, and a long note goes unread' with a concrete moment, e.g. 'At 50 pages, Monday's note is three screens of footer dates and cookie banners, and the one price change is buried on screen two.' Also move the 'Tomorrow…' line from card 9 to the end of the try card so the chapter's last line is the open loop.
